prompt:
Moral Foundations Theory is a framework that separates human morality into the following categories:

  - Care/Harm: related to our long evolution as mammals with attachment systems
    and an ability to feel (and dislike) the pain of others. It underlies the
    virtues of kindness, gentleness, and nurturance.

  - Loyalty/Betrayal: related to our long history as tribal creatures able to
    form shifting coalitions. It is active anytime people feel that it is "one
    for all and all for one." It underlies the virtues of patriotism and
    self-sacrifice for the group.

  - Authority/Subversion: shaped by our long primate history of hierarchical
    social interactions. It underlies virtues of leadership and followership,
    including deference to prestigious authority figures and respect for
    traditions.

  - Sanctity/Purity: shaped by the psychology of disgust and contamination. It
    underlies notions of striving to live in an elevated, less carnal, more
    noble, and more "natural" way (often present in religious narratives). This
    foundation underlies the widespread idea that the body is a temple that can
    be desecrated by immoral activities and contaminants (an idea not unique to
    religious traditions). It underlies the virtues of self-discipline,
    self-improvement, naturalness, and spirituality.

  - Equality: related to our intuitions about equal treatment and equal outcome
    for individuals.

  - Proportionality: related to our intuitions about individuals getting
    rewarded in proportion to their merit or contribution.

TEXT_E:
New Labour presents a modern, non-dogmatic programme for national renewal: a government for the many, not the few, guided by clear values—fairness, opportunity, responsibility—and by the test “what counts is what works.” It rejects both old left statism and Conservative laissez-faire, favouring partnership between government, business and communities to raise standards, restore trust in politics, and unite the country for the challenges of a global, high‑tech economy.

Core commitments
- Clean politics and accountable power: end hereditary voting rights in the Lords; a Freedom of Information Act; incorporate the European Convention on Human Rights; transparent party funding; decentralise to Scotland and Wales (by referendum), create a strategic London authority with a mayor, strengthen local government and consider English regional assemblies where people choose them.
- Economic stability with fairness: low inflation, reformed and more independent monetary policy, the “golden rule” (borrow to invest, not to fund day‑to‑day spending), stick to current spending totals for two years, save to invest—not tax and spend. No rise in basic or top income tax rates; aim for a 10p starting rate; cut VAT on fuel to 5%. A windfall levy on privatised utilities funds a welfare‑to‑work programme.
- Pro‑business, pro‑work modernisation: tougher competition law; a revitalised public–private investment programme; support for small firms, science and green technologies; Regional Development Agencies; a sensibly set National Minimum Wage via a Low Pay Commission; keep key 1980s union law while promoting workplace partnership and the EU Social Chapter to raise employability, not costs.
- Education first: raise the share of national income spent on education; smaller infant class sizes (paid for by ending assisted places); universal nursery places for four‑year‑olds; a laser focus on standards (literacy/numeracy targets, setting by ability); Education Action Zones; teacher quality, a General Teaching Council, trained heads; wire schools to the internet and launch a National Grid for Learning; expand lifelong learning with Individual Learning Accounts and a University for Industry; fair, income‑contingent student support reform.
- Save and modernise the NHS: end the costly internal market; cut red tape and shift money to frontline care; treat 100,000 extra patients quickly and end waits for cancer surgery; primary‑care‑led commissioning, longer‑term agreements, tougher quality standards and a new Patients’ Charter; annual real‑terms funding rises; a public health drive, tobacco ad ban, independent Food Standards Agency.
- Crime and its causes: halve the time to sentence persistent young offenders; final warnings not repeat cautions; more police on the beat; devolve and strengthen the CPS; consistent, tougher sentencing for serious repeat crime; zero tolerance of disorder; victims’ rights; a free vote to ban all handguns; an anti‑drugs coordinator and compulsory treatment pilots.
- Strong families and decent homes: a national childcare strategy; basic working time and parental leave protections; protect Child Benefit; revive social housing using council house receipts; tackle homelessness; fair private renting (licensing HMOs); commonhold. Secure retirement through a protected basic pension (uprated at least with prices), stakeholder pensions, SERPS option retained, and a Royal Commission on long‑term care.
- Environment, culture and transport: every department a “green” department; integrated transport (a new rail authority; PPP for the Underground; safer roads; cleaner vehicles); rural services protected; access to the countryside and stronger animal welfare. Back creativity and sport via NESTA, safeguarding school playing fields, and major event bids. Reform the Lottery for wider public benefit.
- Britain leading in Europe and the world: engage and lead in the EU—complete the single market, reform CAP/CFP, enlarge eastwards, sign the Social Chapter, more open EU governance; consider the single currency by economic tests and referendum. Strong defence through NATO, retain Trident while pursuing multilateral disarmament, ban landmines, a strategic defence review and defence diversification. An ethical, development-led foreign policy: restructure aid under a new Development Secretary, refocus on the poorest, move toward 0.7% of national income, relieve debt, champion human rights, support an international criminal court, and lead on climate change (target a 20% CO2 cut by 2010).

Five early pledges
- Cut infant class sizes to 30 or under by ending assisted places
- Fast-track persistent young offenders
- Cut NHS waiting lists by 100,000 using £100m saved from red tape
- Get 250,000 under‑25s off benefit and into work via a windfall levy
- No rise in income tax rates; cut VAT on heating to 5%; keep inflation and interest rates as low as possible

Britain deserves better; New Labour will deliver practical, radical change with modern means and measurable results.

TEXT_C:
Yes We Can—win the best for Scotland. The SNP’s 1997 manifesto sets out a confident, costed route to independence so Scotland can put its wealth to work for jobs, social justice and world-class public services, free from Westminster’s failed Tory policies and Labour’s timid acceptance of them.

Scotland’s case
- A wealthy nation paying its way: Treasury figures show Scotland has sent £27bn more to London since 1979. With North Sea revenues, Scotland ranks among the richest developed nations.
- Normal nationhood: independence is standard for successful small countries. EU membership continues, open borders with England remain, pensions/investments protected.
- Route to statehood: a majority of SNP MPs triggers negotiations with the UK and EU, followed by a single-question referendum to ratify the settlement, then elections.

Democracy and rights
- A written constitution and Bill of Rights guaranteeing free speech, housing, education, healthcare, decent work and a minimum wage.
- A modern unicameral parliament elected by proportional representation, votes from 16+, strong committees, citizen-initiated bills; reform of the monarchy; entrenched local government (also PR-elected).

Prosperity with fairness
- Full-employment strategy: 100,000 additional jobs via independence, investment, and skills.
- Competitive business taxes: cut corporation tax (main rate to 30p; small companies to 18p), abolish Class IV NICs, fairer business rates, a Scottish Export Unit, and doubled tourism marketing.
- Skills and innovation: National Apprenticeship scheme, Scottish Skills Foundation, R&D support.
- Fair personal taxation: introduce a 15p starter rate, widen the basic-rate band, remove the NI ceiling for high earners; cut VAT on domestic fuel to 5%.
- Adopt the EU Social Chapter; a negotiated minimum wage at half median male earnings; a Charter for Trade Union rights and responsibilities.

Social justice and safety
- NHS rebuilt as an integrated public service—scrap the internal market, reinvest bureaucracy savings, add £35m a year, national audit, dentistry back in the NHS, tobacco ad ban, stronger public health and nutrition.
- End poverty’s grip: raise Child Benefit to £12.50; restore benefits for 16–17s; a Pensioners’ Package—state pension up (£3 single/£5 couples weekly), a universal Cold Climate Allowance, no standing charges for utilities, end means testing for residential care.
- Safer communities: support “zero tolerance” on vandalism and petty crime, stronger Procurator Fiscal service, alternatives to prison where effective, a total ban on handguns, tighter firearms controls.

Education, housing, local services and culture
- 700 extra teachers; repair schools; free nursery education for all 3–4-year-olds; restore student grants; more training places; universal school internet access.
- Tackle the housing crisis: transfer 75% of local authority housing debt to unlock £1.6bn for new homes, renovations and energy efficiency; protect new social homes from discounted Right to Buy; create a new accountable housing agency.
- Restore democratic local control (end quangos, reform finance, PR for councils); bring water back under democracy.
- Culture and sport: a Scottish Broadcasting Corporation (publicly funded) alongside diverse commercial services; equal status for Gaelic and Scots; a reformed, socially responsible Scottish Lottery.

Land, rural Scotland, environment, energy and transport
- Abolish feudal tenure; a transparent Land Register; devolve Crown Estate seashore/seabed to councils.
- Agriculture: Scottish-led BSE recovery (traceability), CAP reform toward working farmers, stronger processing and exports; an independent food and consumer health agency.
- Fisheries: regional management, fair enforcement, stock conservation, processing support.
- Double woodland cover in 25 years; a crofting development agency.
- Strong, independent SEPA; national environmental targets; end nuclear reprocessing at Dounreay and build a renewables R&D hub.
- Energy: fair share of North Sea assets (per existing legal boundary), stable taxation, end the “Great Gas Robbery,” phase out nuclear generation, accelerate renewables and conservation.
- Transport: take Railtrack’s Scottish assets into public ownership; modernise/electrify key rail lines; integrate buses; end punitive bridge tolls (including Skye); strengthen CalMac; abolish H&I Air Passenger Duty; expand direct international links.
- Telecommunications: rural connectivity, distance learning leadership, pro-Internet adoption, modern regulation.

Europe and the world; defence
- Full EU membership with a vote and veto; more MEPs; Scottish EU Presidency in turn; better deals on CFP and CAP.
- Targeted, modern diplomatic presence; UN, Council of Europe, Commonwealth membership.
- Scottish Defence Forces fit for purpose (army, navy, air force), a peacekeeping college, remove Trident, phased NATO withdrawal while maintaining cooperation; defence diversification and Scottish procurement focus.

Paying for it
- A fully costed four-year independence budget shifts resources from nuclear weapons to people’s priorities, funds enterprise and services, grows the economy, and repays national debt. Yes We Can—be independent, prosperous and fair.
